recent_posts.title: Introduction to Rust procedural macros with practical examples
recent_posts.summary: A practical introduction to Rust procedural macros covering all three macro types (derive, function-like, attribute) and both implementation approaches (declarative vs procedural). Walks through building function-like procedural macros step by step: starting with a passthrough 'nothing' macro, then a 'time_this' macro that measures block execution time, and finally a 'hash_set!' macro. Covers key ecosystem crates including proc-macro2, quote, and syn, explains token stream internals (Ident, Punct, Literal, Group token tree variants), and discusses macro hygiene best practices like using scoped blocks and fully qualified paths.

recent_posts.title: Rust Parallelism with Rayon - Use ALL CPUs
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of the Rayon crate for CPU-bound parallelism in Rust. Covers parallel iterators (replacing `.iter()` with `.into_par_iter()`), `rayon::join` for parallelizing non-collection computations, and `rayon::scope` for spawning multiple tasks. Demonstrates an 8x speedup on a 10-million-element workload, explains when parallel iterators hurt performance (small data, low computation cost), and walks through parallelizing binary tree inversion with a depth threshold to avoid excessive queuing overhead. Contrasts Rayon with Tokio, emphasizing Rayon is for synchronous CPU-bound work while Tokio targets async I/O-bound operations.

recent_posts.title: How async Rust and Tokio concurrency actually work under the hood
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of async Rust and Tokio, clarifying common misconceptions about how concurrency and parallelism actually work. Covers the difference between serial execution, concurrent execution with tokio::join!, and true parallel execution with tokio::spawn. Explains how the Tokio multi-threaded runtime uses worker threads, how async functions yield control to the scheduler, and why blocking/synchronous operations inside async tasks are problematic. Also covers spawn_blocking as the correct approach for CPU-bound or blocking work, and demonstrates how combining async I/O with Tokio tasks allows hundreds of concurrent requests on just a few OS threads.

recent_posts.title: Go for TIRED Rust Developers
recent_posts.summary: A satirical but informative comparison of Go and Rust from the perspective of a Rust developer who might be tired of the language's complexity. Covers key differences including Go's lack of a borrow checker, implicit nil handling vs Rust's Option type, simpler pointer usage for recursive types, goroutines vs async/await, built-in channels, and JSON serialization without derive macros. The author ultimately acknowledges both languages are great and the choice comes down to trade-offs.

recent_posts.title: SpacetimeDB Creator On Benchmark Skepticism
recent_posts.summary: The creator of SpacetimeDB defends their benchmarking methodology, arguing that benchmarking databases in isolation is meaningless. What matters is end-to-end application performance — specifically request-to-client response time — which is why they chose to benchmark the full stack (server and database combined) rather than the database alone.

recent_posts.title: How Software Development Might Change
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on how AI and LLMs are changing software development, expressing uncertainty about the future while noting that current AI tools are increasingly handling drudgery and enabling developers to revisit shelved project ideas. The near-term outlook is that developers will be able to build more, faster, rather than being replaced outright.

recent_posts.title: Where AI Generated Code Isn't Good Enough
recent_posts.summary: A database company shares its practical experience with AI-assisted development. While AI-generated code isn't reliable enough for core database features, it excels at repetitive tasks like reviewing code for documentation consistency and testing how well documentation performs by having an LLM build sample applications from it. This feedback loop helps improve documentation quality and ultimately user experience.

recent_posts.title: A Long Term Vision For the Cloud
recent_posts.summary: A vision for reimagining cloud computing as a single giant computer — an OS-level abstraction where developers simply submit programs and the cloud handles all scheduling, replication, networking, and resilience automatically. SpacetimeDB is presented as a step toward this future, using a table-centric interface instead of file-centric (like Unix) to embed more application logic at the OS layer with real-time sync built in.

recent_posts.title: SpacetimeDB's real value is architectural simplicity not just performance
recent_posts.summary: SpacetimeDB's core value proposition goes beyond raw performance. The real benefit is architectural simplicity: instead of maintaining separate servers for chat, audio, video, payments, and user state (each with their own synchronization logic), SpacetimeDB lets developers unify all application state into a single table-based model, eliminating the complexity of coordinating multiple specialized backend services.

recent_posts.title: SpacetimeDB 2.0 benchmark numbers vs Node and PostgreSQL
recent_posts.summary: SpacetimeDB 2.0 demonstrates dramatic performance improvements over traditional Node.js + PostgreSQL stacks. Benchmarks show 4,000 transactions per second with Node/Postgres versus 104,000 TPS with SpacetimeDB, and up to 167,000 TPS when reducers are written in Rust — roughly a 40x improvement.
